title: Erdős Problem #1084: Unit Distances Among Separated Points
description: Let f_d(n) be the maximum number of unit-distance pairs among n points in ℝ^d with all pairwise distances ≥ 1. For d=2, Harborth gave the exact formula. For d=3, Erdős conjectured f_3(n) = 6n - Θ(n^{2/3}). Status: OPEN (d ≥ 3).

meta.assumptions: 1 axiom: maxUnitDistPairs. Structure fields are object definitions, not assumptions.

sections.title: Imports and Setup
sections.summary: Imports from Mathlib: `InnerProductSpace.Basic` for the Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{R}^d$, `Data.Real.Sqrt` for $\sqrt{12n-3}$ in Harborth's formula, and general tactics.

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.summary: Defines `SeparatedConfig d n` (points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with pairwise distance $\ge 1$), `unitDistPairs` (edge count of unit-distance graph), and $f_d(n) = \max$ unit pairs over all configurations.

sections.title: One-Dimensional Case: $f_1(n) = n-1$ (Machine-Verified)
sections.summary: Specialized `SeparatedConfig1D` in $\mathbb{R}$. **Machine-verified**: triangle lemma ($|x-y|=|x-z|=1, |y-z|\ge 1 \Rightarrow |y-z|=2$), degree bound ($\deg \le 2$), upper bound ($\le n-1$), and achievability ($\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ gives $n-1$ pairs via explicit injection).
sections.mathContext: Proved: $f_1(n) = n - 1$. Triangle lemma, degree $\leq 2$, forest bound, and constructive achievability via consecutive integers.

sections.title: Two-Dimensional Case
sections.summary: Erdős's bound $f_2(n) < 3n - c\sqrt{n}$, Harborth's exact formula $f_2(n) = \lfloor 3n - \sqrt{12n-3} \rfloor$ (1974), triangular lattice optimality, and the trivial bound $f_2(n) < 3n$ from kissing number $\tau(2) = 6$.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős introduced this problem in 1946, asking how many 'contacts' (unit-distance pairs) can occur among n non-overlapping unit spheres in ℝ^d. The problem connects sphere packing theory, the classical Newton–Gregory kissing number dispute (1694), and extremal graph theory. For d = 2, the kissing number τ(2) = 6 gives f₂(n) ≤ 3n; Harborth (1974) found the exact formula f₂(n) = ⌊3n - √(12n-3)⌋ using the triangular lattice A₂, one of the most elegant results in combinatorial geometry. For d = 3, Newton proved τ(3) = 12 (confirmed by Schütte–van der Waerden 1953), giving f₃(n) ~ 6n. Bezdek and Reid (2013) proved the n^{2/3} correction: f₃(n) < 6n - 0.926·n^{2/3}, establishing the surface-to-volume isoperimetric deficit for finite sphere packings. The matching lower bound remains open and is related to the Kepler conjecture (Hales 2005). In high dimensions, the Kabatyansky–Levenshtein bound (1978) gives τ(d) ≤ 2^{0.401d}, but the true behavior of f_d(n) for large d remains mysterious.
overview.problemStatement: Estimate f_d(n), the maximum number of unit-distance pairs among n points in ℝ^d with pairwise distances ≥ 1.
overview.text: Let f_d(n) be the maximum number of unit-distance pairs among n points in ℝ^d with all pairwise distances ≥ 1. For d=2, Harborth gave the exact formula. For d=3, Erdős conjectured f_3(n) = 6n - Θ(n^{2/3}). Status: OPEN (d ≥ 3).
overview.proofStrategy: The Lean formalization defines separated configurations and unit-distance pair counting in arbitrary dimension d. For d = 1, four theorems are machine-verified: the triangle lemma (unit neighbors must be on opposite sides), the degree bound (at most 2 unit neighbors), the upper bound (at most n-1 unit pairs, via left-endpoint injection), and the achievability theorem (the consecutive integer configuration {0,1,...,n-1} achieves exactly n-1 unit pairs, proved via an explicit bijection with Fin(n-1)). The d = 2 and d = 3 results are formalized as axioms capturing Harborth's formula, the Bezdek-Reid bound, and Erdős's conjecture. General dimension bounds use kissing number estimates.
keyInsights: **Kissing number controls the leading coefficient**: $f_d(n) \le \tau(d) \cdot n / 2$ by double-counting. Known values $\tau(1) = 2$, $\tau(2) = 6$, $\tau(3) = 12$ give leading terms $n$, $3n$, $6n$
**Harborth's formula** $f_2(n) = \lfloor 3n - \sqrt{12n-3} \rfloor$ encodes the boundary deficit of the hexagonal lattice — one of the few exact extremal results in combinatorial geometry
**Isoperimetric exponent** $n^{2/3}$ in $d = 3$ reflects the surface-to-volume ratio: a ball of volume $n$ has surface area $\Theta(n^{2/3})$, and surface spheres lose contacts

**Four machine-verified theorems** for d=1: the triangle lemma, the 3-neighbor impossibility, the upper bound (at most n-1 unit pairs), and the achievability of n-1 unit pairs via consecutive integers — establishing f₁(n) = n-1 constructively
**Exponential gap** in general $d$: between $f_d(n) \ge dn$ from $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and $f_d(n) \le 2^{O(d)} n$ from Kabatyansky–Levenshtein — closing this is a major open problem
prerequisites: Euclidean geometry: distance in $\mathbb{R}^d$, inner product spaces
Combinatorial geometry: kissing numbers, sphere packing, lattices
Graph theory: degree bounds, extremal graph counting
Familiarity with Lean 4 and Mathlib's EuclideanSpace API

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #1084 asks for the maximum number of unit-distance pairs among separated points. The problem is fully solved for d = 1 (f₁(n) = n - 1, with key lemmas machine-verified) and d = 2 (Harborth's elegant formula using the triangular lattice). For d = 3, the leading coefficient 6 is established via the kissing number τ(3) = 12, and Bezdek–Reid proved the n^{2/3} correction in the upper bound, but the matching lower bound — Erdős's conjecture f₃(n) = 6n - Θ(n^{2/3}) — remains open.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: Understanding f_d(n) precisely would reveal the fine structure of finite sphere packings, connect to the Kepler conjecture and sphere packing rigidity, and illuminate the transition between lattice and non-lattice optimal packings.

The exponential gap between upper and lower bounds in high dimensions is intimately connected to the long-standing open problem of determining the kissing number τ(d) for large d.
openQuestions: Is f₃(n) = 6n - Θ(n^{2/3})? Specifically, does the lower bound f₃(n) ≥ 6n - c₁·n^{2/3} hold?
What are the exact constants c₁, c₂ in the 3D correction term?
Is there an exact formula for f₃(n) analogous to Harborth's 2D result?
Can the exponential gap between f_d(n) ≥ dn and f_d(n) ≤ 2^{O(d)}·n be closed for large d?
Does the optimal configuration for f₃(n) converge to FCC/HCP packing as n → ∞?

crossReferences.description: The Kepler conjecture (FCC sphere packing optimality) governs f₃(n) asymptotics: the conjectured lower bound f₃(n) ≥ 6n - Θ(n^{2/3}) follows from finite FCC/HCP clusters approaching the infinite-volume limit
Studies unit distances without the separation constraint. Problem #1084 adds the ≥1 separation condition, converting a graph-theoretic extremal problem into a sphere-packing one
Asks for the minimum number of distinct distances among n points in ℝ^d. Both use dimension-indexed f_d(n) and exhibit isoperimetric correction terms of order n^{(d-1)/d}
Neighboring extremal combinatorial geometry problem (Erdős-Purdy, 1971) on triangles of equal area, sharing incidence-geometry toolkit (Szemerédi-Trotter)
Distance multiplicity in point configurations: the kissing-number constraint τ(2) = 6 driving f₂(n) ≤ 3n also bounds equidistant vertices in convex position

references.citation: Harborth, H. (1974). Lösung zu Problem 664A. Elemente der Mathematik, 29, 14–15.
references.note: Proves the exact formula f₂(n) = ⌊3n - √(12n-3)⌋ for separated points in ℝ², showing the triangular lattice A₂ is optimal.

references.citation: Bezdek, K. and Reid, S. (2013). Contact graphs of unit sphere packings revisited. Journal of Geometry, 104(1), 57–83.
references.note: Establishes the upper bound f₃(n) < 6n - 0.926·n^{2/3} using the isoperimetric method for finite sphere packings in ℝ³.

references.citation: Kabatyansky, G. A. and Levenshtein, V. I. (1978). Bounds for packings on the sphere and in space. Problemy Peredachi Informatsii, 14(1), 3–25.
references.note: Provides the exponential upper bound τ(d) ≤ 2^{0.401d} on kissing numbers in d dimensions, giving the upper bound f_d(n) ≤ 2^{O(d)}·n.

references.citation: Erdős, P. (1946). On sets of distances of n points. American Mathematical Monthly, 53(5), 248–250.
references.note: Foundational paper introducing the problem of unit distances among n points, the precursor to the separated-points variant formalized here.

references.citation: Schütte, K. and van der Waerden, B. L. (1953). Das Problem der dreizehn Kugeln. Mathematische Annalen, 125, 325–334.
references.note: Resolves the Newton–Gregory kissing number dispute by proving τ(3) = 12, establishing the leading coefficient 6 in f₃(n) ~ 6n.

mainTheorems.name: unit_distance_1d_triangle
mainTheorems.description: In R, if two points are both at unit distance from a third with all pairwise distances >= 1, they are distance 2 apart (opposite sides)

mainTheorems.name: unit_distance_1d_degree_at_most_two
mainTheorems.description: A point in R cannot have 3 unit-distance neighbors among mutually separated points (degree bound <= 2)

mainTheorems.name: f1_upper_bound
mainTheorems.description: For any 1D separated config on n points, the number of unit-distance pairs is at most n - 1

mainTheorems.name: f1_achievable
mainTheorems.description: The consecutive integer configuration {0, 1, ..., n-1} achieves exactly n-1 unit-distance pairs

mainTheorems.name: harborth_exact
mainTheorems.description: Harborth's formula: f_2(n) = floor(3n - sqrt(12n-3)) for separated points in R^2, optimal on triangular lattice

mainTheorems.name: erdos_1084_d3_conjecture
mainTheorems.description: The d=3 conjecture: f_3(n) = 6n - Theta(n^{2/3}), with leading coefficient from the kissing number tau(3) = 12
